wool.origin: Wool is the fleece fiber of the domestic sheep (Ovis aries); Merino is one breed line within that species. Merino genetics were long controlled by the Spanish crown, which banned export of the sheep before 1765, after which selected flocks went to Saxony and elsewhere. Merino descended from a Spanish royal flock reached Australia at the end of the eighteenth century, and Australian fine-wool growing later became a large export industry. Today fine apparel wool is traded internationally as greasy fleece, scoured wool and combed top.
wool.structure: Wool is a keratin composite. An outer cuticle of overlapping scales, arranged like roof shingles, surrounds a cortex of spindle-shaped cortical cells held together by a lipid and protein cell membrane complex. Inside each cortical cell, alpha-helical keratin intermediate filaments about 7.5 nm across are embedded in a matrix of keratin-associated proteins, some rich in cystine (high-sulfur) and some rich in glycine and tyrosine. Oxidized cystine forms disulfide cross-links that stabilize the matrix. In fine Merino the cortex is bilateral: orthocortex and paracortex sit side by side, the paracortex carrying more cystine, and the orthocortex lies on the outer side of each crimp wave, which is the structural basis of crimp.
wool.process: Sheep are shorn, and fleeces are skirted to remove stained edges and classed by fineness, length and color. Scouring in warm detergent baths removes wool grease (the source of lanolin), suint salts and dirt. Carding opens the fiber into a web. On the worsted route the sliver is gilled and combed to remove short fiber (noil), producing parallel top for smooth, compact yarn; on the woollen route carded fiber is condensed and spun directly for bulky, lofty yarn. Machine-washable (superwash) wool is commonly produced by the chlorine-Hercosett route, in which chlorination degrades scale edges and a polyamide-epichlorohydrin resin then coats the fiber.
wool.performance: Wool is hygroscopic, with moisture regain commonly given at roughly 14 to 18% under standard conditions (65% RH, 20 C), and it releases heat of sorption as it absorbs water vapor. It has a limiting oxygen index of about 25 and an ignition temperature of about 570 to 600 C in Woolmark and CSIRO data, and it chars rather than melting or dripping. The directional frictional effect of the scales lets fibers ratchet toward their root ends under heat, moisture and agitation, which causes felting shrinkage. As an amphoteric protein, wool takes acid, metal-complex and wool-reactive dyes. Keratin-digesting clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae are its main pests.
wool.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done with care: wool usually burns slowly, smells like burning hair, tends to self-extinguish and leaves a brittle, crushable black residue. Under a light microscope, the cuticle scale pattern is diagnostic of an animal fiber. Scanning electron microscopy uses scale height at the scale edge as an objective criterion to separate sheep wool from specialty fibers such as cashmere, and DNA and proteomic methods are used when fiber blends or heavily processed fabrics are in dispute.
wool.labeling: In the US, the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 (15 U.S.C. 68 et seq.) and the FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 300 govern wool labeling. The statute defines wool as fiber from the fleece of sheep or lamb or hair of the Angora or Cashmere goat, optionally including the specialty fibers of camel, alpaca, llama and vicuna, never reclaimed from a woven or felted product. Under EU Regulation 1007/2011, 'fleece wool' or 'virgin wool' is reserved for wool never previously incorporated in a finished product. The IWTO Fabric Labelling Code of Practice governs 'Super S' terms, and the Textile Exchange Responsible Wool Standard prohibits mulesing on certified farms.
wool.past: Spain's merino flocks underpinned a fine-wool monopoly until the crown began releasing animals in the later eighteenth century; Saxony received a royal consignment in 1765 and Saxon breeders turned the Merino toward extremely fine wool. Merino descended from a flock that King Carlos III had given to the House of Orange reached New South Wales in 1797, and John Macarthur, aided by large land grants, built flocks whose fine wool rivaled Spanish and Saxon supply. By the late nineteenth century wool was Australia's leading export. In recent decades mulesing, a surgical procedure against flystrike, has become a central welfare controversy that shaped certification schemes.
facts: about 18.75 microns mean fiber diameter under the IWTO code; each step of 10 is about 0.5 micron finer
